topic: Chemistry — Chemical bonds, ionic, covalent and metallic
subject: combined-science

items.q: The specification describes covalent bonding in terms of which particles?
items.correct: atoms which share pairs of electrons
items.misconception: ions which have swapped electron pairs
items.why: The phrase sharing electrons is used so often as a general description of bonding that it is applied to all three types. Sort the three types by what happens to the outer electrons: ionic transfers them, covalent shares pairs between two atoms, metallic shares delocalised electrons across the whole structure.
items.random_wrong: atoms sharing delocalised electrons

items.q: Which of these is a compound held together by ionic bonding?
items.correct: lithium fluoride, a metal and a non-metal
items.misconception: sulfur dioxide, a compound of two elements
items.why: Ionic bonding is taught first and is often introduced simply as what happens when two elements combine. The outcome - a compound - sticks, while the condition that one element must be a metal is dropped. Check the periodic table first. Metal plus non-metal gives ionic bonding; non-metal plus non-metal gives covalent bonding.
items.random_wrong: hydrogen chloride, a gas containing chloride

items.q: Covalent bonding occurs in which of these?
items.correct: most non-metallic elements and non-metal compounds
items.misconception: compounds of non-metals only, never in elements
items.why: Bonding is introduced through reactions, so students associate a bond with a chemical change between different elements and never look inside an element. Chlorine gas is Cl2: two atoms sharing a pair of electrons, a covalent bond. The two atoms being the same makes no difference.
items.random_wrong: any compound made from two different elements

items.q: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Which type of bonding does it have?
items.correct: metallic, because alloys bond like pure metals
items.misconception: ionic, because it contains two different elements
items.why: The rule metal plus non-metal is remembered as two elements combined, so any two-element substance is filed as ionic. Both copper and zinc are metals. Neither will accept electrons, so no ions form. The atoms share delocalised electrons - metallic bonding.
items.random_wrong: ionic, since positive ions attract negative ions

items.q: In terms of electrostatic forces, what is the ionic bond in sodium chloride?
items.correct: attraction between oppositely charged ions
items.misconception: the movement of an electron across the bond
items.why: Dot and cross diagrams draw an arrow for the transfer, and the arrow is the most eye-catching feature, so it is read as the bond itself. The transfer happens once and is over; what remains is a positive ion and a negative ion attracting each other. That attraction is the bond.
items.random_wrong: a pair of electrons shared by the ions

items.q: Which statement correctly links the three bond types to what happens to the outer electrons?
items.correct: ionic transfers electrons; covalent and metallic share them
items.misconception: all three types involve sharing pairs of electrons
items.why: The phrase sharing electrons is used so often as a general description of bonding that it is applied to all three types. Sort the three types by what happens to the outer electrons: ionic transfers them, covalent shares pairs between two atoms, metallic shares delocalised electrons across the whole structure.
items.random_wrong: ionic and metallic share electrons; covalent transfers

items.q: A magnesium atom reacts with oxygen. What happens to magnesium's outer electrons?
items.correct: they are transferred, giving a 2+ ion
items.misconception: six more are gained for a full outer shell
items.why: The rule full outer shell is remembered without the second half - the easiest route to a full shell. Emptying a nearly empty shell is not considered. Compare the routes: gaining seven electrons or losing one. Losing one is far easier, and the shell below is already full, so Na+ is 2,8.
items.random_wrong: they are lost, giving a 2- charged ion

items.q: Which ions have the electronic structure of a noble gas?
items.correct: those formed by Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7
items.misconception: none, since an ion keeps its structure
items.why: Electronic structure is learned as a property of the element, tied to its place in the periodic table, so it is treated as fixed. The element is set by the number of protons, which never changes. The electrons do change, and that is the whole point of ion formation.
items.random_wrong: only those whose charge equals the group

items.q: A sodium atom, 2,8,1, forms a sodium ion. What is the ion's electronic structure and charge?
items.correct: 2,8 with a charge of 1+, the same as neon
items.misconception: 2,8,8 with a charge of 7-, like argon
items.why: The rule full outer shell is remembered without the second half - the easiest route to a full shell. Emptying a nearly empty shell is not considered. Compare the routes: gaining seven electrons or losing one. Losing one is far easier, and the shell below is already full, so Na+ is 2,8.
items.random_wrong: 2,8,1 with a 1+ charge, shells unchanged

items.q: In a dot and cross diagram of sodium chloride, how is the sodium ion drawn?
items.correct: in brackets with a 1+ charge, outer shell empty
items.misconception: in brackets with a 1+ charge and one outer electron
items.why: The electron is drawn as a cross and can be seen on the chloride side, but students copy the atom diagram out of habit and leave the electron in place on both sides. An electron drawn twice would be two electrons. Draw it once, in the shell it moved to, and put the charges on the brackets.
items.random_wrong: with an arrow showing the electron crossing over

items.q: Which dot and cross diagram represents magnesium chloride?
items.correct: one Mg2+ ion drawn with two Cl- ions
items.misconception: one Mg2+ ion drawn with a single Cl- ion
items.why: Sodium chloride is met first, where one to one works, so pairing one ion with one ion becomes the default. The total positive charge must cancel the total negative charge. One 2+ needs two 1- ions.
items.random_wrong: one Mg2+ ion drawn with a Cl7- ion

items.q: Which pairing of group and ionic charge is correct?
items.correct: Group 6 forms an ion with a 2- charge
items.misconception: Group 6 forms an ion carrying a 6- charge
items.why: Group number is correctly linked to charge for Groups 1 and 2, where the two numbers happen to be equal, and the rule is then carried straight across to Groups 6 and 7. For Groups 6 and 7 the charge is the number of electrons still needed: 8 minus the group number. Group 6 gains 2, Group 7 gains 1.
items.random_wrong: Group 2 forms an ion with a charge of 2-

items.q: Calcium is in Group 2 and fluorine in Group 7. Which pair of ions do they form?
items.correct: Ca2+ and F-, since calcium loses two
items.misconception: Ca2+ and F7-, taken from the group numbers
items.why: Group number is correctly linked to charge for Groups 1 and 2, where the two numbers happen to be equal, and the rule is then carried straight across to Groups 6 and 7. For Groups 6 and 7 the charge is the number of electrons still needed: 8 minus the group number. Group 6 gains 2, Group 7 gains 1.
items.random_wrong: Ca2- and F+, as calcium gains electrons

items.q: Potassium is in Group 1 and oxygen in Group 6. What is the formula of the compound formed?
items.correct: K2O, as two 1+ ions balance one 2- ion
items.misconception: KO, because one ion of each is enough
items.why: Sodium chloride is met first, where one to one works, so pairing one ion with one ion becomes the default. The total positive charge must cancel the total negative charge. One 2+ needs two 1- ions.
items.random_wrong: K6O, read from the two group numbers

items.q: What holds an ionic compound together?
items.correct: strong electrostatic forces between charged ions
items.misconception: strong bonds pointing from each ion to its partner
items.why: The stick in a ball and stick model, and the line in a displayed formula, both show bonding as a link between exactly two particles. Electrostatic attraction is not a line. A positive ion attracts every negative ion around it, in every direction, throughout the lattice.
items.random_wrong: pairs of electrons shared between the ions

items.q: Why does the specification say that the forces in an ionic lattice act in all directions?
items.correct: each ion attracts oppositely charged ions around it
items.misconception: each ion is bonded to one partner ion only
items.why: Formulae for small molecules such as H2O are met first and do describe one molecule, so the same reading is applied to an ionic formula. Each sodium ion in the lattice is attracted to six chloride ions and vice versa. No ion has one partner, so no NaCl molecule exists.
items.random_wrong: the bonds point along fixed lines like sticks

items.q: A diagram shows a regular cube of alternating small and large spheres, one element a metal. What is it?
items.correct: a giant ionic lattice with the ions alternating
items.misconception: separate molecules of the compound stacked up
items.why: Formulae for small molecules such as H2O are met first and do describe one molecule, so the same reading is applied to an ionic formula. Each sodium ion in the lattice is attracted to six chloride ions and vice versa. No ion has one partner, so no NaCl molecule exists.
items.random_wrong: a metal, its atoms in a random jumble

items.q: Which of these is a limitation of a ball and stick model of sodium chloride?
items.correct: the sticks suggest gaps between the ions
items.misconception: it shows the compound as separate molecules
items.why: Formulae for small molecules such as H2O are met first and do describe one molecule, so the same reading is applied to an ionic formula. Each sodium ion in the lattice is attracted to six chloride ions and vice versa. No ion has one partner, so no NaCl molecule exists.
items.random_wrong: it shows forces in two directions only

items.q: A model of an ionic compound shows 8 magnesium ions and 16 chloride ions. What is the empirical formula?
items.correct: MgCl2, the simplest whole number ratio
items.misconception: Mg8Cl16, the numbers counted in the model
items.why: Counting atoms works for molecules, where the count is the formula, so the same counting is carried over to a fragment of a lattice. A lattice has no fixed size, so the count depends on where the model stops. Reduce the numbers to the simplest ratio.
items.random_wrong: MgCl, since the ions pair up one to one

items.q: Water boils at 100 C. What does this tell you about the covalent bonds within a water molecule?
items.correct: nothing; the bonds in it are strong
items.misconception: they are weak, since water boils easily
items.why: One number, the boiling point, is used to judge every force present, because the difference between forces inside a molecule and forces between molecules has not yet been drawn. Ask what is being pulled apart. Boiling pulls whole molecules apart from one another; the H-O bonds inside each molecule survive intact.
items.random_wrong: they break when the water turns to steam

items.q: Which of these substances consists of small molecules?
items.correct: CH4, a compound of two non-metals
items.misconception: NaCl, a short two-symbol formula
items.why: Formula length and the -ide ending are surface features that are quicker to use than checking whether each element is a metal or a non-metal. Look up each element. Sodium is a metal, so NaCl is ionic and giant. Hydrogen and chlorine are both non-metals, so HCl is a small covalent molecule despite its name.
items.random_wrong: SiO2, which looks just like CO2

items.q: Poly(ethene) is a covalently bonded substance with very large molecules. What does that mean?
items.correct: its molecules are very large but separate
items.misconception: it has a giant covalent structure like diamond
items.why: Large is treated as the definition of giant, and the difference between a very large molecule and a structure with no molecules at all is a fine one. Ask whether the substance can be divided into separate molecules. A polymer can - into chains. Diamond cannot.
items.random_wrong: the covalent bonds in it must be weaker

items.q: Which pair of substances both have giant covalent structures?
items.correct: diamond and silicon dioxide, the named examples
items.misconception: carbon dioxide and silicon dioxide, two oxides
items.why: Formulae are used as the main clue to structure, and these two look identical, so the same structure is assumed. SiO2 is an empirical formula for a giant structure, not a molecule. The specification names silicon dioxide as a giant covalent structure.
items.random_wrong: poly(ethene) and diamond, both very large

items.q: In the representation of a polymer, what does n stand for?
items.correct: a large number of repeating units
items.misconception: a number you work out from the diagram
items.why: Every other letter in a formula stands for a value that can be found, so n is treated as an unknown to be calculated. Polymer chains vary in length even within one sample, so there is no single value of n. The specification states only that n is a large number.
items.random_wrong: the count of carbon atoms in the unit

items.q: How many shared pairs of electrons are there between the atoms in an oxygen molecule, O2?
items.correct: two, drawn as four electrons in the overlap
items.misconception: one, since a covalent bond is one shared pair
items.why: The definition of a covalent bond as a shared pair is learned from hydrogen and hydrogen chloride, where one pair is all there is. Count what each atom still needs. Oxygen needs two more electrons, so it must share two pairs; nitrogen needs three, so it shares three.
items.random_wrong: four, one for each electron in the overlap

items.q: In the displayed formula of methane, what does each of the four lines represent?
items.correct: one single bond, that is one shared pair
items.misconception: one electron passed from carbon to hydrogen
items.why: A line looks like a single item, and dot and cross diagrams show individual electrons, so the line is matched to one electron rather than to a pair. Convert between the two pictures: every line in a displayed formula is a pair of electrons in the dot and cross diagram.
items.random_wrong: the two electrons carbon contributes

items.q: What is a limitation of a two-dimensional displayed formula of a methane molecule?
items.correct: it does not show the real shape of the molecule
items.misconception: it shows the atoms at their true relative size
items.why: Models are handled as physical objects and photographed in textbooks, so their features are taken to be features of the substance. Treat every model as showing one thing well and other things badly. Ball and stick shows the arrangement; a space-filling model shows how the ions actually pack.
items.random_wrong: it gives the ratio of atoms, not the number

items.q: A model of ethene shows two black balls (carbon), four white balls (hydrogen) and six sticks. What is the molecular formula?
items.correct: C2H4, counting only the balls
items.misconception: CH2, the simplest whole number ratio
items.why: The rule about simplest whole number ratios is learned for empirical formulae of giant structures and is then applied to molecules as well. Molecules have a definite number of atoms, so the molecular formula records that number. Simplifying is only for empirical formulae.
items.random_wrong: C2H6, one hydrogen for each stick

items.q: How are the atoms arranged in a pure metal?
items.correct: in a giant structure with a regular pattern
items.misconception: randomly, in a closely packed jumble of atoms
items.why: The word delocalised, and the idea of electrons moving freely, is extended from the electrons to the metal ions themselves. The ions stay in a regular pattern; only the delocalised electrons move. That regular pattern is why metals form crystals.
items.random_wrong: a lattice of positive and negative ions

items.q: Which statement about the electrons in a metal is correct?
items.correct: the outer electrons are free to move about
items.misconception: each atom keeps its outer electrons, loosely
items.why: Shell diagrams always show electrons belonging to one atom, and that picture is kept when metals are met. Delocalised means no longer belonging to any one atom. The electrons form a sea that all the metal ions sit in.
items.random_wrong: every electron in every atom is delocalised

items.q: In terms of electrostatic forces, what is a covalent bond?
items.correct: attraction between the shared pair and both nuclei
items.misconception: an electron moving from one atom to the other
items.why: Dot and cross diagrams draw an arrow for the transfer, and the arrow is the most eye-catching feature, so it is read as the bond itself. The transfer happens once and is over; what remains is a positive ion and a negative ion attracting each other. That attraction is the bond.
items.random_wrong: attraction between the two positive nuclei

items.q: What gives rise to the strong metallic bonds in copper?
items.correct: attraction between metal ions and delocalised electrons
items.misconception: attraction between positive and negative ions
items.why: The plus signs in the standard diagram are read as evidence of ionic bonding, since that is the only place plus signs have been seen before. Ionic bonding needs a non-metal to take the electrons. In a metal nothing takes them - they are shared by every atom at once.
items.random_wrong: shared pairs of electrons between two metal atoms

items.q: A magnesium atom loses two electrons. Is the ion negative?
items.correct: No. Losing negative electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion is Mg2+, positively charged.
items.misconception: Losing something makes you go down, so losing electrons should give a negative charge.
items.why: Loss is associated with less and with minus signs, and the charge that is actually lost is negative, so the signs get crossed. Count the charges. Magnesium has 12 protons and 12 electrons. Remove two electrons and 12 positives face 10 negatives, so the ion is 2+.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When reading a formula from a ball and stick model, do you count the sticks?
items.correct: No. The formula comes from counting the balls, which are the atoms. The sticks show the bonds.
items.misconception: Every stick joins something on, so the sticks should be counted as part of the formula.
items.why: Sticks are the most obvious feature of the model and are the same colour as nothing else, so they are read as another kind of particle. Count only the balls, sorting them by element, then write the symbols with the counts as subscripts.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In the dot and cross diagram of hydrogen, how many bonds are shown?
items.correct: One. The two electrons in the overlap - one dot and one cross - are a single shared pair, so one covalent bond.
items.misconception: Each atom puts in an electron and each of those electrons is a bond, so there are two bonds.
items.why: The two symbols in the overlap look like two separate things, and the phrase each atom contributes an electron encourages counting them one at a time. Count pairs, not electrons. Two electrons in the overlap make one shared pair, which is one covalent bond.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are all of the electrons in a metal delocalised?
items.correct: No. Only the electrons in the outer shell of the metal atoms are delocalised.
items.misconception: The whole atom breaks up in a metal, so every electron it has joins the sea.
items.why: The sea of electrons picture is drawn without any inner shells, so the remaining positive particles look like bare nuclei. The specification is specific: the electrons in the outer shell are delocalised. The inner shells stay with their own nucleus.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does boiling water break the covalent bonds in the molecules?
items.correct: No. Boiling separates whole water molecules from one another. The covalent O-H bonds inside each molecule are not broken.
items.misconception: Water turns into steam, so the bonds holding the molecules together must have broken apart.
items.why: Change of state is described as particles separating, and the only bonds a student has drawn for water are the covalent ones, so those are the bonds assumed to break. Steam is still H2O. If the covalent bonds had broken, hydrogen and oxygen gas would be produced instead.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
